leads.text: Unbounded recursive redirect following in `_http_get` (src/picklescan/scanner.py:240-259) gives server-controlled SSRF plus uncontrolled recursion. The function signature is `def _http_get(url) -> bytes:` -- a single parameter, with NO redirect counter, depth limit, or host allow-list anywhere in the body. On `if response.status == 302:` (line 251) it does `return _http_get(response.headers["Location"])` (line 252), where the `Location` header is entirely controlled by the remote server. The recursive call re-enters `urllib.parse.urlparse(url)` (243) and builds a brand-new connection from the NEW host: `http.client.HTTPSConnection(parsed_url.netloc)` (246) then `conn.request("GET", path_and_query)` (248). Two consequences: (1) SSRF -- any host the user scans can 302-redirect picklescan to an arbitrary attacker-chosen `netloc`, including internal/loopback/link-local addresses, and the response body is then fed to `scan_bytes`; note the scheme from `Location` is discarded entirely because `HTTPSConnection` is hardcoded, so the redirect target host is always contacted over HTTPS regardless of what scheme the attacker supplies. (2) Uncontrolled recursion -- a server returning a 302 loop (or a long redirect chain) drives unbounded recursion into RecursionError / stack exhaustion. Attacker-controlled entry: `cli.py:66 scan_url(args.url)` -> `scanner.py:611 _http_get(url)`, and `cli.py:68 scan_huggingface_model(args.huggingface_model)` -> `scanner.py:561/572 _http_get(...)`.

leads.text: Remote-JSON-controlled filename injected into the download URL in `scan_huggingface_model` (src/picklescan/scanner.py:557-573). The HTTP response body from `https://huggingface.co/api/models/{repo_id}` is parsed with `json.loads(...)` (line 561) and each `sibling.get("rfilename")` value from `model["siblings"]` is collected into `file_names` (line 562) with no validation beyond a `is not None` check. The same unvalidated `file_name` also flows into `os.path.splitext(file_name)` (line 567) to pick `file_ext`, which selects the parser used in `scan_bytes(data, url, file_ext)` (line 573), letting the remote JSON steer which scan branch handles the downloaded bytes. leads.text: DELIBERATELY DISABLED ZIP INTEGRITY CHECK: `RelaxedZipFile.open` (src/picklescan/relaxed_zipfile.py:19) is a copy of CPython's `zipfile.ZipFile.open` with the local-header-vs-central-directory filename consistency check REMOVED. The method still reads the local file header (line 77 `fheader = zef_file.read(sizeFileHeader)`), validates header length (line 78) and the PK\003\004 magic (line 81-82), and reads the filename and extra-field bytes (lines 84-86) — but it then DISCARDS the filename bytes without ever comparing them to `zinfo.orig_filename`, whereas upstream CPython raises `BadZipFile('File name in directory %r and header %r differ.')`. Confirmed repo-wide: no call anywhere references `orig_filename` or `fname`. This creates a scanner/consumer parser differential: `scan_zip_bytes` selects which entries to scan from `zip.namelist()` (central directory) and decides the handler via `os.path.splitext(file_name)[1]`, while a downstream unzip implementation that honours the local-header name may extract different content under a different name — so an archive with deliberately mismatched names is accepted and scanned by picklescan instead of being rejected as malformed.

leads.text: src/picklescan/relaxed_zipfile.py:90-91 explicitly disables ZIP CRC integrity validation with the hedge comment "# Disable CRC validation as PyTorch may not use it" followed by `zef._expected_crc = None`. RelaxedZipFile.open is a vendored copy of CPython's zipfile.ZipFile.open, and it is the ONLY zip reader picklescan uses for archive scanning (scanner.py:444 `RelaxedZipFile(data, "r")` inside scan_zip_bytes). Because _expected_crc is nulled, zipfile.ZipExtFile.read() will never raise BadZipFile on a checksum mismatch, so the bytes picklescan disassembles as a pickle are never authenticated against the archive's own stored checksum. A crafted archive can therefore present member content that picklescan parses and declares clean while a stricter/different consumer of the same archive reconstructs or rejects different bytes. The node is reachable_from_entry=true, and the project ships a fixture (tests/init_data_files.py:453 initialize_corrupt_zip_file_crc, which rewrites b"print('456')" to b"print('123')" to force a CRC mismatch) plus tests/test_scanner.py:385 assert_scan("malicious1_crc.zip", ...) that locks this disabled-check behavior into the test suite.

leads.text: src/picklescan/relaxed_zipfile.py:84-88 — the vendored RelaxedZipFile.open removes CPython ZipFile.open's local-header/central-directory consistency checks. It reads the local file header's filename bytes and DISCARDS them (`zef_file.read(fheader[_FH_FILENAME_LENGTH])`, with no assignment to `fname`), then goes straight to `zipfile.ZipExtFile(...)` at line 88. Absent relative to upstream CPython: (a) `if fname_str != zinfo.orig_filename: raise BadZipFile('File name in directory %r and header %r differ.')`, (b) the flag-bit 5 compressed-patch NotImplementedError guard, (c) the flag-bit 6 strong-encryption NotImplementedError guard. Net effect: picklescan locates member data using the LOCAL header's filename/extra-field lengths while taking compress_type/compress_size/CRC from the CENTRAL directory entry (via self.getinfo(name) at line 54), with no cross-check between the two and with CRC off. That is a central-vs-local parser-differential primitive: an archive whose central directory names a benign member at a header_offset whose local header describes something else will be read by picklescan without error, while a loader that trusts local headers reconstructs different content. The class exists solely to weaken stock validation, and tests/init_data_files.py:433 initialize_corrupt_zip_file_central_directory deliberately builds such a divergent archive by replacing b"data.pkl" with b"datap.kl".

leads.text: The literal set of global-producing pickle opcodes recognised by `_list_globals` omits the extension-registry opcodes EXT1/EXT2/EXT4. The only opcode literals that add to the returned `globals` set are `("GLOBAL", "INST")` (scanner.py:291) and `"STACK_GLOBAL"` (scanner.py:293); the remaining opcode literals in the function are memo bookkeeping (`["MEMOIZE","PUT","BINPUT","LONG_BINPUT"]` at 289/296, `["GET","BINGET","LONG_BINGET"]` at 303) and string-type validation (`["SHORT_BINUNICODE","UNICODE","BINUNICODE","BINUNICODE8","STRING","BINSTRING","SHORT_BINSTRING"]` at 325). A full enumeration of every literal collection under src/picklescan/ contains no "EXT1"/"EXT2"/"EXT4" string anywhere. Pickle protocol>=2 EXT1/EXT2/EXT4 resolve a callable through the copyreg extension registry by integer code without emitting any GLOBAL/INST/STACK_GLOBAL opcode, so such a stream yields an empty `globals` set, `_build_scan_result_from_raw_globals` reports issues_count=0, and cli.py:76 returns exit code 0 (clean). Caveat for the verifier: exploitability additionally requires the target code to have a populated copyreg extension registry at load time.

leads.text: Hard-coded magic-number bound in the legacy-PyTorch scan path limits how much of a file is inspected. `scan_pytorch` (scanner.py:501) falls through to the old-format branch and executes `for _ in range(5): scan_result.merge(scan_pickle_bytes(data, file_id, multiple_pickles=False))` — the literal `5` at scanner.py:525 caps the number of sequential embedded pickle streams read from the stream, and `multiple_pickles=False` disables the self-terminating multi-pickle loop inside `_list_globals`. A legacy-format file carrying more than 5 concatenated pickle streams would have the 6th and later streams never disassembled, and the function then hard-sets `scan_result.scanned_files = 1`. Verifier should check whether a legacy torch file with >5 embedded streams is actually loadable by torch (which determines real exploitability).

leads.text: Third-party component inventory (components-with-known-vulnerabilities class): the declared Dependency set is 10 packages. Two observations I can ground from the graph: (a) `numpy` is declared with an unpinned floating range `>1.24.0,<2.0.0` rather than a hard pin, so a build can silently resolve to any 1.24.x-1.26.x release — unlike every other runtime dep here, which uses `==`; numpy is loaded inside the security-relevant `scan_numpy` path (`import numpy as np`, scanner.py:472). (b) the tooling pins `twine==4.0.1` and `flake8==5.0.4`, both markedly older than the rest of the pinned set (`black==24.10.0`, `pytest==8.3.5`, `pytest-cov==6.0.0`); `twine` is the package-publishing tool, so a stale publish toolchain is a supply-chain-relevant staleness. HONEST SCOPE NOTE for the verifier: the runtime pins `requests==2.32.5`, `aiohttp==3.13.3`, `torch==2.8.0`, `py7zr==0.22.0` are all recent and I did NOT find evidence of a known advisory against any of them; I am deliberately NOT asserting any CVE, because nothing in the graph grounds one. This lead is a version inventory requiring an external advisory-database cross-check, not a confirmed vulnerable component.
